evidence.text: We developed and qualified a translational whole-body PBPK model for mRNA-LNP therapeutics that: (i) mechanistically captures saturable endothelial transport and intracellular processing; (ii) reproduces organ-resolved mRNA and protein kinetics in rat; and (iii) scales to human to recapitulate plasma mRNA PK across clinically relevant doses.

Sensitivity analyses identify endosomal degradation, mRNA stability, and translation as the principal determinants of hepatic protein exposure once initial delivery is achieved, and cell-type analyses quantify how potential Kupffer-cell “sink” effects may constrain hepatocyte expression.

Practically, these results prioritize escape/stability engineering over further increases in gross hepatic deposition, and they provide a rational basis for potentially tuning LNP properties to favor desired liver cell types.
Here we report the construction and validation of a whole-body translational PBPK platform for mRNA-LNP therapeutics.
In this modeling framework, pharmacokinetics (PK) refers specifically to mRNA disposition, whereas pharmacodynamics (PD) refers to the resulting encoded protein expression.

Building on the anatomical template of Shah and Betts [15], we introduced Michaelis–Menten infiltration terms to model receptor saturation and receptor mediated tissue infiltration, an endosomal sub-compartment to account for degradation and escape, and mRNA to protein translation within each tissue.
Parameters were calibrated against the comprehensive rat dataset of Ci et al., [22], encompassing both mRNA and translated protein across different organs.

Although the calibration was performed for a specific LNP formulation, the underlying model structure is designed to support re-calibration for other LNP designs, recognizing that differences in chemical composition may alter tissue distribution, cellular uptake, and downstream expression.
The current implementation focuses on intravenous (IV) administration, consistent with the available biodistribution data.

Quantitative receptor measurements (density, turnover) in relevant vascular beds, time-resolved endosomal pH/escape readouts, and single-cell resolved mRNA/protein trajectories would enable replacement of phenomenological terms with mechanistic modules.
Complementary in vitro studies characterizing species-dependent cellular uptake or endosomal processing would further enhance model validation and mechanistic resolution.

On the clinical side, paired early plasma sampling with minimally invasive tissue or soluble-protein biomarkers could help resolve transport vs.

evidence.text: Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models provide a mechanistic framework to integrate those layer-specific processes with species-specific anatomy as well as blood and lymphatic flow [15].
Platform PBPK approaches are established for small molecules and large molecule therapeutics (e.g.
monoclonal antibodies, ADCs, etc.), where they have enabled various decision makings, such as first-in-human (FIH) dose selection, drug-drug interaction assessment and regulatory filings [16, 17].
Emerging in parallel, PBPK frameworks for mRNA-LNP are nascent.

Existing efforts span models focused on the liver [18], organ-specific perfusion models [19], integrated minimal PBPK/QSP models within the context of rare diseases [20], and whole-body PBPK models used to simulate exposure of secreted biologics such as bispecific T cell engagers [21].
evidence.context_after: Our goal was to develop a whole-body PBPK modeling platform to simultaneously capture (i) receptor-mediated, saturable trans-endothelial transport, (ii) intracellular trafficking and translation, and (iii) rigorous inter-species scaling across all major organs.

evidence.text: Beyond liver centric applications, the same framework can be used to (i) explore extrahepatic targeting via alternative lipid compositions and targeting ligands; (ii) simulate complex modalities such as mRNA-encoded bi-specifics or cytokines with feedback on clearance or distribution; and (iii) integrate with QSP pharmacodynamic models to translate tissue protein time-courses into functional PD (e.g., enzyme replacement, immune activation).

Because the model already operates at the organ and cellular-compartment levels, these extensions are largely modular: a receptor-level transport block can be dropped into specific tissues, or a PD block (e.g., target engagement, signal transduction) can be integrated into protein output in a cell-type-resolved manner.

evidence.text: The pharmacokinetics of mRNA-LNP is complex and multi-layered.

After intravenous (IV) administration, the particles encounter a dynamic protein corona that determines opsonization, clearance by the mononuclear phagocyte system and interaction with apolipoprotein E (ApoE) dependent receptors on hepatocytes and endothelial cells [10, 11].
Particle size, ionizable-lipid pKa and helper-lipid composition all modulate this corona and hence tissue tropism [12, 13].

Within target organs the particles must cross the endothelial fenestrae, undergo uptake (often via scavenger or LDL-family receptors), survive endosomal degradation and finally release mRNA into the cytosol where ribosomes translate the mRNA into encoded protein.
Each layer involves distinct rate-limiting steps and can introduce pronounced species differences [14].

Consequently, while conventional allometric approaches remain valuable tools, relying on them without accounting for the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) complexities of mRNA-LNP may lead to less informative or potentially misleading dose projections.
The liver microenvironment analysis using the PBPK model highlights potentially important role of cell-type competition in modulating liver protein expression [23].

Simulations show that increasing LNP uptake into Kupffer cells produces a near-linear rise in Kupffer-cell protein but exerts a modest “sink” effect that can limit interstitial availability and influence hepatocyte expression beyond a threshold consistent with available experimental evidence highlighting the role of Kupffer cells in shaping LNP hepatic distribution [36, 37].

evidence.text: From the standpoint of translational biomarkers, the PBPK platform makes it straightforward to link mechanistic assumptions to measurable surrogates.

For example, if endosomal degradation is a dominant limiter for a given construct, the model predicts pronounced shifts in protein exposure with small changes in escape kinetics—suggesting that modest differences in ionizable lipid composition may manifest as outsized differences in circulating protein (for secreted payloads) or tissue PD (for intracellular targets).

Similarly, when the model is used to generate “what-if” scenarios for receptor saturation, it predicts changes on very early plasma/tissue mRNA time-course, implying that sampling around infusion could be informative for deconvolving transport vs.
intracellular rate limiting steps in FIH studies [20].
In sum, the platform provides a coherent quantitative scaffold for hypothesis testing, construct prioritization, and FIH planning.
